facts.title: The Edge Absent from Band Aid (1984) – Hospitalized with Kidney Infection
facts.body: The Edge was unable to join his bandmate Bono at the recording of "Do They Know It's Christmas?" (Band Aid, 1984) because he was hospitalized at the time with a kidney infection. "Was hospitalized with a kidney infection and could not join Bono at the recording."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts About Music in 40 or so Minutes (2025 Edition)
facts.name: U2

facts.title: Studying Bruce Springsteen's Performance (1984)
facts.body: While gaining prominence, Bono and the rest of U2 closely observed Bruce Springsteen during his "Born in the USA Tour" in 1984. They specifically studied his methods for transforming large-scale songs into even more impactful stadium performances without diminishing their emotional depth. "They watched how he took big songs and made them bigger in stadium setting without diluting all the emotion in those songs."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Influencers - Springsteen
facts.name: U2

facts.title: Infiltrating Pop Culture (1984)
facts.body: By 1984, hip-hop, though still a couple of years from its full pop breakthrough, was significantly infiltrating the zeitgeist. Elements like scratching, rapping, and breaking began "infecting middle of the road 1984 pop records," exemplified by Irene Cara's "Break Dance" and the films "Breakin'" and "Breakin' 2: Electric Boogaloo." "Hip-hop culture becomes pop culture."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: What’s 1984 Got to Do with It Edition Part 1
facts.name: hip hop

facts.title: Emergence of "Beefs" (1984)
facts.body: The rap world saw the emergence of "beefs" or "Dis Records" in late 1984, with releases like Roxanne Shante's "Roxanne, Roxanne" and The Real Roxanne's "Roxanne's Revenge." While the "biggest beef" of the year was a media-concocted rivalry in pop, these rap dis tracks indicated a developing aspect of hip-hop culture. "Rap was also becoming famous for beefs, the Dis Records, Roxanne, Roxanne, and Roxanne's Revenge also dropped in late 84."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: What’s 1984 Got to Do with It Edition Part 1
facts.name: hip hop

facts.title: 1984 as "Pop's Greatest Year"
facts.body: Rolling Stone magazine referred to 1984 as "Pops Greatest Year," highlighting that the year's biggest hit, Prince's "When Doves Cry," was also its most visionary. "Rolling Stone ranking of the greatest hits of what the magazine called Pops Greatest Year, they said of this song, quote, the year's biggest hit was also its most visionary."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2
facts.name: pop

facts.title: 1984 as "Pop's Greatest Year"
facts.body: Rolling Stone magazine, in September 2014, published a feature titled "100 best singles of 1984, pop's greatest year," explicitly calling 1984 the "greatest year" for pop music. The article and broader critical consensus argued that 1984 was exceptional for pop as a centralizing force where rock, R&B, dance, country, and hip hop all found a place on the radio. "Rolling Stone boldly titled the countdown 100 best singles of 1984, pop's greatest year."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: What’s 1984 Got to Do with It Edition Part 1
facts.name: pop

facts.title: Formation and Name Origin (1984)
facts.body: The Tragically Hip formed in 1984 in Kingston, Ontario, with Gord Downie (20 years old at the time), Gord Sinclair, Robbie Baker, Johnny Faye, and sax player Dave Manning (about 15 years older). They took their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape called "Elephant Parts," produced by video pioneer Michael Nesmith (formerly of The Monkees). The phrase "tragically hip" also appears in Elvis Costello's 1982 song "Town Cryer" from the "Imperial Bedroom" album. "Things started coming together in 1984 when Gord, then 20 years old, the other Gord, Robbie, Johnny Faye, and a sax player, about 15 years older than everyone named Dave Manning, formed the tragically hip, taking their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape making the rounds called Elephant Parts."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Gord Downie - Canada's Rock Poet
facts.name: The Tragically Hip

facts.title: Formation (1984)
facts.body: The Tragically Hip was formed in 1984 when Gord Downie reconnected with Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair at Queen's University. They recruited high school student Johnny Fay on drums and a more experienced saxophone player from British Columbia named Davis Manning. "This was 1984."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Gord Downie: A Remembrance-Part 1
facts.name: The Tragically Hip

facts.title: British Airways Lawsuit (1984)
facts.body: The Beastie Boys sued British Airways after the airline allegedly used a sample from their song "Beastie Revolution" (likely referring to "Cookie Puss") in a worldwide commercial without permission. The band won a judgment for $40,000, which marked the first money they ever made from music. They used these funds to rent an apartment and rehearsal space at 99 Christie Street. "The Beastie Boys heard it in New York in the cinema, and sued British airways. It was the first money they ever made out of music."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering the Beastie Boys Part 1
facts.name: The Beastie Boys

facts.title: Madonna's Tour Opener (1984)
facts.body: Madonna selected the Beastie Boys to open for her 1984 *Like a Virgin* tour. She had originally wanted Run DMC, but they were too expensive, making the Beasties a more affordable alternative for the gig, which came about through a mix-up with Russell Simmons. "Madonna, who threw a mix up with Simmons, ended up with the Beastie Boys as her opener for her 1984-like a virgin tour."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering the Beastie Boys Part 1
facts.name: The Beastie Boys

facts.title: Conservative Backlash to Like A Virgin (1984)
facts.body: With the release of the "Like A Virgin" album and Madonna's increasingly radical and explicit image, significant controversy erupted. Conservative elements, "rancid politicians," and Catholic movements began to express their disapproval, perceiving her content as inappropriate. "Los elementos conservadores, los políticos rancios, los movimientos católicos y a todos empiezan a ver que eso no está bien."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Madonna y la provocación
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: MTV Music Awards 1984 Performance - The Scandal
facts.body: At the first MTV Music Awards in 1984, Madonna delivered a highly scandalous and historic performance. She emerged from a giant cake wearing a wedding dress identical to her "Like A Virgin" album cover, complete with the "Boy Toy" belt, and proceeded to dance provocatively, rolling and writhing on the floor, creating a major sensation in the United States. "Viene el escándalo, viene el momento histórico de Madonna porque Madonna actúa y la lia a parla."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Madonna y la provocación
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Manager's Reaction to MTV Performance (1984)
facts.body: Freddy DeMann, Madonna's manager at the time, reacted to her scandalous 1984 MTV Music Awards performance with extreme concern. He famously exclaimed, "Oh my God, it's the end of her career!" believing the controversial act would ruin her future prospects. "Freddy Demand, el que era humana y artes, que decía, ¡Ay Dios mío, es el final de su carrera!"
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Madonna y la provocación
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: MTV Director's Reaction to MTV Performance (1984)
facts.body: The director of the MTV Awards in 1984 was profoundly distressed by Madonna's provocative performance. He feared it would be the first and last MTV Awards gala, considering whether to cut the transmission immediately, and didn't know how to react to the unfolding scandal. "Pensé que era la primera y la última gala de los MTV Awards porque con eso no le iba a dejar transmiter ninguna otra gala al resto de su vida."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Madonna y la provocación
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Post-MTV Performance Media Explosion (1984)
facts.body: Immediately following her scandalous 1984 MTV Music Awards performance, Madonna's fame exploded. The very next day after the broadcast, she was ubiquitous, appearing in newspapers, magazines like Vogue, and on the radio, dominating media coverage. "Madonna estaba en todas partes. Madonna salió en los periódicos, salió en las revistas, salió en la revista Vogue, salió en la bandeja en las radios."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Madonna y la provocación
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Ultra-Catholic Protests (1984)
facts.body: In the wake of Madonna's provocative 1984 MTV Music Awards performance and her rising controversial image, ultra-Catholic groups initiated protests. They gathered outside her home and at the record label's headquarters, attempting to organize boycotts against her. "Empezaban las protestas ultra católicos a la puerta de su casa, en la puerta de la discográfica, empezaban a intentar hacerle boycots."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Madonna y la provocación
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Archetypal Imperial Phase (1984-1989)
facts.body: Madonna's 5-year chart run from 1984 through 1989 is considered an unprecedented, potentially unrepeatable, and archetypal "Imperial Phase." This period saw her achieve a remarkable streak of top five hits that lasted throughout the 1980s, beginning with "Lucky Star" and "Like a Virgin." "But Madonna's 5-year run of hits from 1984 through 1989, which I submit was one long Imperial phase checks a lot of the boxes."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 2
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Fashion Icon Status Established (1984)
facts.body: The music video for her single "Lucky Star" was instrumental in establishing Madonna as a fashion icon, with her lacy, naval-bearing outfit inspiring a multitude of "Madonna wannabes" and marking a pivotal moment in her early career. "First, the video for her next single, Lucky Star, the final hit from the debut album, established Madonna as a fashion icon, with a lacy, naval-bearing outfit that would inspire scores of Madonna wannabes."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 2
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Debut Performance at MTV VMAs (September 1984)
facts.body: Madonna delivered the "most talked about performance" at the inaugural MTV Video Music Awards in September 1984, debuting "Like a Virgin" while famously arriving on stage in a disheveled bridal gown. This performance was a key factor in her transformation into "80s pop's new Imperial Queen." "Madonna delivered the most talked about performance at the first MTV Video Music Awards in September of 1984."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 2
facts.name: Madonna

"Empezaban las protestas ultra católicos a la puerta de su casa, en la puerta de la discográfica, empezaban a intentar hacerle boycots."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Madonna y la provocación
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Archetypal Imperial Phase (1984-1989)
facts.body: Madonna's 5-year chart run from 1984 through 1989 is considered an unprecedented, potentially unrepeatable, and archetypal "Imperial Phase." This period saw her achieve a remarkable streak of top five hits that lasted throughout the 1980s, beginning with "Lucky Star" and "Like a Virgin." "But Madonna's 5-year run of hits from 1984 through 1989, which I submit was one long Imperial phase checks a lot of the boxes."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 2
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Fashion Icon Status Established (1984)
facts.body: The music video for her single "Lucky Star" was instrumental in establishing Madonna as a fashion icon, with her lacy, naval-bearing outfit inspiring a multitude of "Madonna wannabes" and marking a pivotal moment in her early career. "First, the video for her next single, Lucky Star, the final hit from the debut album, established Madonna as a fashion icon, with a lacy, naval-bearing outfit that would inspire scores of Madonna wannabes."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 2
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Debut Performance at MTV VMAs (September 1984)
facts.body: Madonna delivered the "most talked about performance" at the inaugural MTV Video Music Awards in September 1984, debuting "Like a Virgin" while famously arriving on stage in a disheveled bridal gown. This performance was a key factor in her transformation into "80s pop's new Imperial Queen." "Madonna delivered the most talked about performance at the first MTV Video Music Awards in September of 1984."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 2
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: "Stop Making Sense" Concert Film (1984)
facts.body: Director Jonathan Demme captured Talking Heads' *Speaking in Tongues* stage show on film, released in 1984 and named *Stop Making Sense*, after a lyric from their song "Girlfriend Is Better." It was a "decent box office performer" and is now "widely considered the greatest concert film of all time." It helped establish Talking Heads as an "American institution." "They named the movie, released in 1984, after a lyric from the funk rock single Girlfriend is better."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2
facts.name: The Talking Heads

facts.title: Integration into Manchester Sound (1984-1986)

facts.title: Band's Peak and Internal Strife (1984)
facts.body: After achieving significant success within just over five years of recording, The Police experienced intense internal exhaustion. The band was characterized by three headstrong personalities, and constant bickering was fueled by Andy Summers's and Stuart Copeland's envy of Sting's prolific and hit-packed songwriting. Even the band's producers found the tension exhausting. "The three headstrong personalities coupled with Andy Summers and Stuart Copeland's envy of Sting's prolific hit-packed songwriting led to constant bickering that even the band's producers found exhausting."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: If You Love Sting, Set Him Free Edition Part 1
facts.name: The Police

facts.title: Permanent Hiatus (1984)
facts.body: Following the conclusion of their Synchronicity tour in the summer of 1984, The Police quietly went on a hiatus without any public fanfare. This hiatus ultimately became permanent, as the band never formally announced a breakup but also never recorded another full-length album together. "After finishing their synchronicity tour in the summer of 84, with no fanfare, the police went on a hiatus that turned out to be essentially permanent."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: If You Love Sting, Set Him Free Edition Part 1
facts.name: The Police

facts.title: Breakup and Hiatus (1984)
facts.body: The Police quietly broke up in 1984 after becoming "Rock's biggest band," going on hiatus before Sting fully embarked on his solo career. "The police have quietly broken up after becoming Rock's biggest band."

facts.title: Fandom and Joining Red Hot Chili Peppers (1984-1988)
facts.body: At 15, around 1984 when the Red Hot Chili Peppers released their debut album, John Frusciante became a dedicated fan, attending their shows and hoping to speak with guitarist Hillel Slovak. He learned all of their songs. Following Slovak's death in June 1988, and Jack Irons' subsequent departure, Frusciante, then 17, began attracting attention for his guitar skills. He turned down an offer from Frank Zappa due to Zappa's anti-drug stance, briefly joined L.A. punk band Thelonius Monster, but ultimately joined the Chili Peppers in October 1988, after a jam session with Flea. "Legend says that he was three hours into his membership with him, when the Chili Peppers called and said, okay, you got the gig. This was October 1988."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1
facts.name: John Frusciante

facts.title: The Works (1984) - "I Want To Break Free" Videoclip
facts.body: Creatively, "The Works" is one of Queen's most questioned albums, but it yielded the visually epic music video for "I Want To Break Free." The video features all band members in drag, famously including Freddie Mercury vacuuming while crossing a doorway. The humor and impact came from seeing other band members like Roger Taylor and Brian May in drag, breaking taboos prevalent in the 1980s. The video also contains other memorable moments, such as a scene interpreted as a version of ancient Greek bacchanalian feasts, showcasing a graphically interesting aesthetic. "Lo divertido no era a Freddy Mercury travestido, era a ver los a los otros."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.name: Queen

facts.title: The Works (1984) - "I Want To Break Free" Videoclip
facts.body: Creatively, "The Works" is one of Queen's most questioned albums, but it yielded the visually epic music video for "I Want To Break Free." The video features all band members in drag, famously including Freddie Mercury vacuuming while crossing a doorway. The humor and impact came from seeing other band members like Roger Taylor and Brian May in drag, breaking taboos prevalent in the 1980s. The video also contains other memorable moments, such as a scene interpreted as a version of ancient Greek bacchanalian feasts, showcasing a graphically interesting aesthetic. "Lo divertido no era a Freddy Mercury travestido, era a ver los a los otros."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica

facts.title: Vehicular Manslaughter of Razzle (1984)
facts.body: In 1984, Vince Neil and Razzle, the drummer for Hanoi Rocks, left a party in Neil's powerful 1972 Ford Pantera to get more alcohol. While driving 65 mph in a 25 mph zone, Neil hit a wet patch, crossed into oncoming traffic, and crashed into two cars. Razzle died in the hospital, and Neil suffered cuts and cracked ribs. "While going 65 in a 25 miles per hour zone, the Pantera hit a wet patch of pavement, it crossed over into the opposite lane and crashed into two cars traveling the other way."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: Ira Kaplan and Georgia Hubley, who formed the indie group Yo La Tengo in 1984, first met at shows and record shops in New Jersey. facts.title: Hardcore Opera
facts.body: Released in the summer of 1984, this double set is considered Hüsker Dü's greatest album and a hardcore opera. It tells the story of a young kid who runs away from a troubled home, only to find life on the outside even worse. His journey includes joining the military, trying religion, and witnessing his girlfriend become a junkie, ultimately concluding that it was all a dream. This album represented a huge evolutionary leap for punk by combining the power and energy of hardcore with melody and more conventional song structures, sometimes incorporating piano and acoustic guitars. "Husker Do's greatest album was this concept record, Zen Arcade, a double set which came out in the summer of 1984."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rock Concept Albums: Part 1
facts.name: Zen Arcade

facts.body: Released in 1984, this album is considered highly significant for the development of emo. It demonstrated that American hardcore could incorporate melody and meaningful lyrics while still being played very fast and loud. The band also experimented with tape effects, acoustic instruments, and vocal harmonies, and introduced deeply personal and emotional lyrical themes. Many observers have compared its impact on emo to that of The Beatles' "White Album." "In 1984, they released a very important album called Zen Arcade. This record showed it was possible for American hardcore to be played very, very fast and very, very loud, but with melody and with meaningful lyrics."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 3: Emo
facts.name: Zen Arcade

facts.title: Groundbreaking Concept Album
facts.body: This 1984 double record was a concept album, a format considered extremely "uncool" and typically avoided by punk and hardcore bands, often associated with groups like Pink Floyd. Hüsker Dü broke through this rigid hardcore dogma by creating a fast, aggressive, and nuanced album that tells the story of a boy who runs away from an abusive home only to find the outside world is even worse. "The group thought hardcore had hit a wall, so it was time to try different things. The music was fast and aggressive, but it was also loaded with nuance. And it was a concept album, something that punk and hardcore bands were just not supposed to do."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: History of Pop Punk: Part 1
facts.name: Zen Arcade

facts.title: Double Concept Album
facts.body: Considered Hüsker Dü's greatest indie achievement, this 1984 double album was a concept record that told the story of a young runaway discovering that the real world was harsher than his home life. It played a significant role in defining what would become alternative rock. "Hustler Doe's greatest indie achievement was a 1984 double album called Zen Arcade, a record that went a long way towards creating what would be categorized as alternative rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Hardcore
facts.name: Zen Arcade

facts.title: Recording "Do They Know It's Christmas?" (November 25, 1984)
facts.body: Just two weeks after Bob Geldof saw the BBC documentary on the Ethiopian famine, 25 of Britain's most renowned musicians assembled at Sarm Studios in London's Notting Hill area on November 25, 1984. They gathered to record the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?", which marked the official beginning of the Band-Aid project. "On November the 25th, 1984, just two weeks after that BBC broadcast, 25 of Britain's most famous musicians gathered at Sarm studios in the Notting Hill area of London to crank out a song that was now called Do They Know It's Christmas?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3
facts.name: Band Aid

facts.title: Live Soundtrack LP
facts.body: The live soundtrack album for the concert film of the same name, released in 1984. It initially saw modest chart success, peaking at number 41, lower than the band's five previous LPs. However, it became a "long-distance runner," staying on the Billboard album chart for nearly two years—longer than any other Talking Heads album—and eventually went double platinum, serving as a de facto greatest hits compilation before the band released any official one. "But Stop Making Sense was the long-distance runner of their albums, serving as a de facto Talking Heads greatest hits, years before the group put out any such compilation."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Cold War Songs 1984 – OMD "Enola Gay," Rush "Distant Early Warning," Pink Floyd, Nena
facts.body: In addition to Frankie Goes to Hollywood's "Two Tribes," the nuclear fears of 1984 generated anti-war protest songs including "Red Skies" by The Fix, "Enola Gay" by OMD, "Two Suns in the Sunset" from Pink Floyd, "99 Luftballons" by Nena, and "Distant Early Warning" from Rush. This was a period when the US and USSR genuinely came close to nuclear conflict on multiple occasions. "It was a very scary time."

facts.body: Released on June 4, 1984, this album features a cover photo of Bruce's backside in well-worn jeans, with a cap sticking out of his pocket and the American flag in the background, signaling a different, less solemn sound than its predecessor, "Nebraska." The song's verses tell a poignant story of a young man from a hometown jam being sent to war, killing "the yellow man," and returning home to unemployment and a dismissive VA, detailing a betrayal of American veterans rather than a patriotic anthem. It reached number nine on the Billboard Hot 100 in the fall of 1984 and was named number 59 out of the top 365 songs of the 20th century by the Recording Industry Association of America. "Born in the USA made it to number nine on the billboard hot 100 in the fall of 1984 the recording industry association of America named it number 59 out of the top 365 songs of the 20th century."

facts.title: Songwriting Collaboration
facts.body: The lyrics for the Band-Aid charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" were notably written by Bob Geldof in the back of a taxi. Midge Ure of Ultravox then took one of Geldof's half-finished songs, originally titled "It's My World," and composed the music, completing the collaborative effort. "Mid-Jour took one of Bob's half-finished songs called It's My World and created the music."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3
facts.name: Do They Know It's Christmas?

facts.title: Chart Success and Sales
facts.body: Released on December 7, 1984, the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" quickly achieved immense success. It entered the UK charts at number one on December 15th and held that position for five weeks, selling over three million copies in the UK alone, making it one of the biggest-selling UK singles ever. Additionally, it sold one million copies in the US. This commercial success marked the significant beginning of Band-Aid as a major charitable endeavor. "On December the 15th, it entered the charts at number one, and it stayed there for five weeks, selling more than three million copies, making it one of the biggest selling UK singles of all time."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3
facts.name: Do They Know It's Christmas?

facts.title: All-Star British Charity Single
facts.body: This 1984 All-Star British charity single aimed to provide relief for the starving in Ethiopia. Sting was given a showcase slot, harmonizing with Duran Duran's Simon LeBon, and organizer Bob Geldof humorously had Sting sing the line "The Bitter Sting of Tears." "On the 1984 All-Star British charity single, do they know its Christmas by band aid? Sting was given a showcase slot, harmonizing with Durandoran's Simon LeBon."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: If You Love Sting, Set Him Free Edition Part 2

facts.title: Inspiration for Band-Aid (November 11, 1984)
facts.body: On the evening of November 11, 1984, after a difficult day attempting to publicize The Boomtown Rats' album "In the Long Grass," Bob Geldof watched a BBC documentary by reporter Michael Buerk detailing the famine in Ethiopia. Deeply affected by the images of starvation, Geldof felt compelled to take action, leading to the inception of the Band-Aid project. "Bob was stunned by the images of starving people, and he was suddenly moved to do something, anything to help these poor people."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3
facts.name: The Boomtown Rats
